MR1947_Diner.head: Diners 115-120
text: The Olympian Hiawatha took over the Chicago - Seattle/Tacoma run on June 29, 1947: a Brooks Stevens styled streamliner on the Milwaukee Road's Pacific Extension, much of it under electric wire across the Rockies and Cascades. Most cars came from the Menomonee Valley shops; the sleepers and Skytop sleeper-lounges came from Pullman-Standard in 1948-49. The train was never a money-maker against the Great Northern and Northern Pacific, and it was withdrawn in May 1961.

The Olympian diners, series 115-120, are among the best documented cars in this fleet. Their plan comes from Milwaukee Public Library drawing A-4224 revision N, corrected to the finished car on 8-16-47. Diagonal seating for 48 fills the dining room; the kitchen sits at the A end behind high oblong windows and short service doors, and a steward's compartment and linen lockers are at the B end. The body is the same as the 1948 Twin Cities diners (A-4836).
To check: window and door heights, which are estimated; number 115 is used as the default.

text: On May 29, 1948 - thirteen years to the day after the first Hiawatha - the Milwaukee Road put new Brooks Stevens styled Morning and Afternoon Hiawathas into service between Chicago and the Twin Cities, built almost entirely by its own Milwaukee Shops. From 1955 the fleet was repainted in Union Pacific Armour Yellow and Harbor Mist Gray, the scheme these models wear.

The Twin Cities diners, 121-126, share their body with the Olympian diners of 1947. The plan is MPL drawing A-4836: kitchen at the A end with high oblong windows and short service doors, six 3'-8" dining windows a side, a steward's compartment at the B end and a kitchen exhaust housing on the roof.
To check: window and side-door heights (estimates); number 121 is the default.

MR1942_TipTopTap.head: The 1942 Tip Top Tap

Two new Tip Top Tap cars were built. The model treats them as full lounge cars; they may instead have been baggage-tap cars like the earlier ones.
To check: the arrangement (full lounge or baggage-tap) and the numbers.

MR1947_TapLounge.head: Tap-Lounge 165

Number 165 was retired in 1971, ran later on the Michigan Star Clipper dinner train, and is privately owned today - a Flickr album documents it.
To check: the layout. It is taken from a Walthers O scale kit drawing and is approximate.

MR1948_Coach.head: The coach that carried the Hiawatha
text: On May 29, 1948 - thirteen years to the day after the first Hiawatha left Chicago - the Milwaukee Road put brand-new Morning and Afternoon Hiawathas into service between Chicago and the Twin Cities. The trains were styled by Milwaukee industrial designer Brooks Stevens and, like every Hiawatha before them, most of the cars were not bought from a car builder at all: they were designed and welded together by the railroad's own people at the Milwaukee Shops in the Menomonee Valley.

The coach was the car most passengers knew. Each one seated 52 in reclining seats in a single long room, with a lounge and washroom at either end - the two oval windows on each side mark them. Twelve wide windows with rounded corners light the seating, and a porthole in each vestibule door is the Brooks Stevens touch that ties the coach to the Skytop observation car at the rear of the train. The sides are smooth welded steel with one thin rib just under the window sills and another just above the window tops; the ends carry rows of horizontal ribs, and an air-conditioning housing sits on the roof over one end.

The new cars were delivered in the Milwaukee Road's own orange and maroon. In 1952 the full-length Super Domes joined both trains, and from 1955 - when the Milwaukee Road took over the Union Pacific's 'Cities' streamliners between Chicago and Omaha - the fleet was repainted in Union Pacific Armour Yellow and Harbor Mist Gray with red striping. That is the scheme this model wears: yellow sides, gray roof, ends and lower band, and a red pinstripe above the band and under the eave.

A Twin Cities Hiawatha of the 1950s ran its coaches behind the express, mail and tap-lounge cars and ahead of the Super Dome, diner, Valley-series parlor cars and Skytop Lounge. The coaches outlasted most of what ran with them. The Afternoon Hiawatha came off on January 23, 1970; the Morning Hiawatha made its last run on April 30, 1971, the day before Amtrak took over the nation's passenger trains.

About the numbers: the Walthers kit roster lists the 52-seat Twin Cities Hiawatha coaches as 535-551, and other published lists differ in detail, so treat any single number as something to check before lettering a car. This model's window layout was measured from a Walthers HO model of the 1948 coach (body 290 mm, 82.9 scale feet) and its ribbed end from the Walthers O scale end casting, not from a railroad drawing.

MR1947_BaggageDorm.head: A home for the crew
text: The Olympian Hiawatha took over the Chicago - Seattle/Tacoma run on June 29, 1947: a Brooks Stevens styled streamliner on the Milwaukee Road's Pacific Extension, much of it under electric wire across the Rockies and Cascades. The train was never a money-maker against the Great Northern and Northern Pacific, and it was withdrawn in May 1961.

A two-day run needed a crew that could sleep aboard. The baggage-dormitory car put a baggage room behind one wide sliding door with a porthole, and a crew dormitory with four windows and two portholes for toilet and shower.
The model is lettered as 1516 and laid out from a three-quarter photo by fitting perspective, so the positions are approximate. The 80 ft length is a best guess, and the far side is assumed to match.
To check: Don's Depot lists a baggage-dorm 1310 - find which series and numbers ran on the Olympian.

MR1952_SuperDome.head: The Super Domes
text: In 1952 Pullman-Standard delivered ten Super Domes, 50-59 - the first full-length dome cars. The dome ran nearly the length of the car, with 68 seats upstairs, a 28-seat lounge below and 625 sq ft of glass. At 224,000 lb they needed reinforced three-axle trucks.
Two ran in each Twin Cities Hiawatha and others on the Olympian Hiawatha. In 1964 six were sold to Canadian National.
To check: which cars went to CN, and the dome glazing pattern for the model's dome glass.

MR1937_BaggageTap.head: The Tip Top Tap, second edition
text: The first Hiawatha was such a success that its cars were too small within two years. In 1937 the Milwaukee Shops turned out a complete new nine-car train - baggage-Tip Top Tap, four coaches, a diner and three parlors including a new Beaver Tail - and the 1935 cars moved down to secondary trains.

The new baggage-Tip Top Tap kept the 1935 idea - baggage forward, a tap lounge aft - but in a longer, heavier car with ribbed sides. The model gives it seven ribs, the same pattern as the 1930s branchline cars.
To check: car numbers, and whether the 1937 sides really carried seven ribs.

MR1935_Coach.head: A lightweight coach from the railroad's own shops
text: On May 29, 1935 the Milwaukee Road started the Hiawatha between Chicago, St. Paul and Minneapolis: about 410 miles in six and a half hours, behind new streamlined Class A 4-4-2 Atlantics built for sustained running at 100 mph. The cars were not bought from Pullman or Budd - they were designed and welded together in the railroad's own Milwaukee Shops, in the Menomonee Valley, a lightweight-car programme the shops had begun in 1934.

The coaches were the heart of the train. Built light and welded rather than riveted, they had smooth sides, a single vestibule and a continuous band of windows - a clean look meant to match the shrouded Atlantic up front. When the 1937 train arrived, the 1935 coaches were bumped to other trains, including the branch and North Woods services.
To check: car numbers, seating capacity and window count. The model uses the fleet's coach template.

MR1935_Parlor.head: Extra-fare comfort on the first Hiawatha
text: On May 29, 1935 the Milwaukee Road started the Hiawatha between Chicago, St. Paul and Minneapolis: about 410 miles in six and a half hours, behind new streamlined Class A 4-4-2 Atlantics built for sustained running at 100 mph. The cars were not bought from Pullman or Budd - they were designed and welded together in the railroad's own Milwaukee Shops, in the Menomonee Valley, a lightweight-car programme the shops had begun in 1934.

Parlor cars carried the extra-fare passengers in individual swivel chairs, with the windows set closer together than in the coaches so that each chair had its own view. They ran just ahead of the Beaver Tail parlor-observation at the rear of the train.
To check: the names and numbers of the 1935 parlors and their chair count.

MR1937_Diner.head: The Hiawatha gets a full diner
text: The first Hiawatha was such a success that its cars were too small within two years. In 1937 the Milwaukee Shops turned out a complete new nine-car train - baggage-Tip Top Tap, four coaches, a diner and three parlors including a new Beaver Tail - and the 1935 cars moved down to secondary trains.

The 1937 train carried a full dining car, with large dining-room windows and small kitchen windows at one end. Meals on a 6 1/2-hour run were a selling point, and the diner was where the railroad showed off.
To check: numbers, and whether the diner rode on four- or six-wheel trucks.

MR1948_RPO.head: RPO 2155
text: On May 29, 1948 - thirteen years to the day after the first Hiawatha - the Milwaukee Road put new Brooks Stevens styled Morning and Afternoon Hiawathas into service between Chicago and the Twin Cities, built almost entirely by its own Milwaukee Shops. From 1955 the fleet was repainted in Union Pacific Armour Yellow and Harbor Mist Gray, the scheme these models wear.

The Railway Post Office car is modelled as 2155 ('was 1511') from drawing A-8028, the stencilling arrangement - which gives the paint as well as the shape: Armour Yellow body, Harbor Mist Gray roof and bottom strip, and 3 in bright red stripes. Lettering on the car named Carl F. Rank.
The car is about 65.7 ft long, with 35'-0" between door openings and four small high windows in the mail room. Walthers models 2152-2153 as a 63 ft RPO.
To check: who Carl F. Rank was (possibly a postal official honoured on the car), and the build date.

MR1947_Touralux.head: Touralux - an economy sleeper
text: The Olympian Hiawatha took over the Chicago - Seattle/Tacoma run on June 29, 1947: a Brooks Stevens styled streamliner on the Milwaukee Road's Pacific Extension, much of it under electric wire across the Rockies and Cascades. Most cars came from the Menomonee Valley shops; the sleepers and Skytop sleeper-lounges came from Pullman-Standard in 1948-49. The train was never a money-maker against the Great Northern and Northern Pacific, and it was withdrawn in May 1961.

Touralux was the Milwaukee Road's answer to passengers who wanted a bed without paying for a room: an open-section sleeper at a lower fare. Fourteen sections each have one big window a side, with a vestibule and porthole side door at the A end and a blind B end.
The model is laid out from photos of 5745 Mt. Rushmore, preserved at Montevideo, Minnesota. The cars were probably numbered 5740-5751.
To check: the numbers; the 82'-10" shop-shell length (a best guess); window heights.

MR1934_Coach4400.head: The first welded coach
text: Coach 4400 is where the Hiawatha cars began. Two of these coaches left the Milwaukee Shops on 3 February 1934 and went into service on trains 5 and 6 between Chicago and the Twin Cities. The body was welded from steel sheet with no rivets, tubular in shape with a turtle-back roof and sides rounded in below the windows. It was the same size as the standard steel coach - a 72 ft 6 in body with a vestibule at each end, 80 ft in all - but weighed about 96,000 lb instead of 146,000 lb. In 1934 it was shown at the Century of Progress exposition in Chicago as the 'Progress Coach'.

It seated 40 in rotating, reclining seats, with a men's smoking room for nine and a ladies' lounge for five. The windows were single sheets of plate glass, oval at the top and square at the bottom. Railway Mechanical Engineer published its floor plan and cross-section in October 1934; the model is drawn from those.
To check: the windows at the women's lounge end (not in the photos) and the rounded upper window corners, which are not modelled yet.

MR1947_RPOBaggage.head: Mail for the Pacific Northwest
text: The Olympian Hiawatha took over the Chicago - Seattle/Tacoma run on June 29, 1947: a Brooks Stevens styled streamliner on the Milwaukee Road's Pacific Extension, much of it under electric wire across the Rockies and Cascades. Most cars came from the Menomonee Valley shops; the sleepers and Skytop sleeper-lounges came from Pullman-Standard in 1948-49. The train was never a money-maker against the Great Northern and Northern Pacific, and it was withdrawn in May 1961.

Mail paid many of the bills for long-distance trains. This RPO-baggage car carries a 30 ft Railway Post Office apartment - mail door, small high barred windows, letter cases and a sorting table - ahead of a baggage room.
To check: which RPO-baggage cars actually ran on the Olympian Hiawatha. This is a generic starting point.

MR1942_Coach.head: A wartime coach
text: By 1942 the Hiawathas were carrying record wartime crowds, with trains of up to fifteen cars. The shops built a partial re-equipment - new coaches, two diners and two Tip Top Tap cars - that ran together with the 1939 parlors and finned Beaver Tails.
The 1942 coaches were among the last new cars before wartime controls stopped passenger-car building. The model gives them Kuhler-style ribbed sides to match the 1939 cars they ran with.
To check: whether the 1942 coaches were ribbed or smooth, and their numbers.

MR1937_Coach.head: Four coaches for a bigger train
text: The first Hiawatha was such a success that its cars were too small within two years. In 1937 the Milwaukee Shops turned out a complete new nine-car train - baggage-Tip Top Tap, four coaches, a diner and three parlors including a new Beaver Tail - and the 1935 cars moved down to secondary trains.
Four coaches ran in each 1937 train - double the seats of 1935. They kept a single vestibule and gained ribbed sides, the first visible break from the smooth 1935 look.
To check: numbers, seating and window count.

MR1935_BaggageBuffet.head: The car that started the Tip Top Tap
text: On May 29, 1935 the Milwaukee Road started the Hiawatha between Chicago, St. Paul and Minneapolis: about 410 miles in six and a half hours, behind new streamlined Class A 4-4-2 Atlantics built for sustained running at 100 mph. The cars were not bought from Pullman or Budd - they were designed and welded together in the railroad's own Milwaukee Shops, in the Menomonee Valley, a lightweight-car programme the shops had begun in 1934.

At the head of the train, behind the locomotive, rode a combined baggage and buffet car. The forward part carried baggage and express; the rear held a buffet and tap lounge - the first of the 'Tip Top Tap' lounges that became a Hiawatha trademark and gave their name to cars for the next thirteen years.
The first Hiawathas wore a scheme of gray, orange and maroon with smooth sides; the fluted and ribbed looks came later.
To check: the exact 1935 head-end arrangement and the car numbers. This model's layout is a generic baggage-tap template, not taken from a drawing.

MR1937_Parlor.head: Parlor cars, 1937
text: The first Hiawatha was such a success that its cars were too small within two years. In 1937 the Milwaukee Shops turned out a complete new nine-car train - baggage-Tip Top Tap, four coaches, a diner and three parlors including a new Beaver Tail - and the 1935 cars moved down to secondary trains.
Two regular parlors ran ahead of the Beaver Tail, giving three extra-fare cars in the train. They followed the 1935 parlors' close window spacing in the new ribbed body.
To check: the parlor names and chair counts.

MR1937_Diner102.head: Seven diners for the Olympian, 1937
text: In July and August 1937 the Milwaukee Shops built seven 48-seat lightweight diners, 102-108, for the transcontinental Olympian, at $38,969 each. They ran with heavyweight cars, so they kept standard diaphragms, and their dining-room and corridor windows were wider than on the Hiawatha diners 100-101. Diner 102 entered service on 21 July 1937; from 103 on, three kitchen windows became double-sash for ventilation and ice and storage boxes were added under the corners of the car - changes later made to 102 as well.
To check: kitchen roof duct and vents, and the corridor-side window positions.

MR1948S_Diner101.head: Diner 101 after re-sheeting
text: From 1948 to 1950 the Milwaukee Road shops re-sheeted the lower sides of the 1934-1942 Hiawatha cars still in service - new lower side sheets with two extra ribs and straight skirting - to stiffen the bodies and prolong their life.
Book p. 148 shows the car as re-sheeted.
To check: the rib heights and the skirt depth against the drawing.

MR1948S_Diner113.head: Diners 113-114 after re-sheeting
text: From 1948 to 1950 the Milwaukee Road shops re-sheeted the lower sides of the 1934-1942 Hiawatha cars still in service - new lower side sheets with two extra ribs and straight skirting - to stiffen the bodies and prolong their life.
Book p. 162 shows the car as re-sheeted.
To check: the rib heights and the skirt depth against the drawing.

MR1939_Diner.head: Dining on the 1939 Hiawatha
text: For 1938-39 the Milwaukee Road hired industrial designer Otto Kuhler to restyle the Hiawatha. The shops built a new train with heavily ribbed sides, and the Atlantics gave way to Kuhler-shrouded Class F7 4-6-4 Hudsons. In January 1939 the railroad split the service into a Morning and an Afternoon Hiawatha, so two full trainsets were needed.
Each Kuhler train carried a full diner in the same ribbed body as the coaches.
To check: numbers and truck type.

MR1939_Parlor.head: A Kuhler parlor
text: For 1938-39 the Milwaukee Road hired industrial designer Otto Kuhler to restyle the Hiawatha. The shops built a new train with heavily ribbed sides, and the Atlantics gave way to Kuhler-shrouded Class F7 4-6-4 Hudsons. In January 1939 the railroad split the service into a Morning and an Afternoon Hiawatha, so two full trainsets were needed.
The parlors ran just ahead of the finned Beaver Tail, giving the rear of the train a run of extra-fare cars.
To check: names and chair counts.

MR1939_BaggageTap.head: Kuhler's Tip Top Tap
text: For 1938-39 the Milwaukee Road hired industrial designer Otto Kuhler to restyle the Hiawatha. The shops built a new train with heavily ribbed sides, and the Atlantics gave way to Kuhler-shrouded Class F7 4-6-4 Hudsons. In January 1939 the railroad split the service into a Morning and an Afternoon Hiawatha, so two full trainsets were needed.

Otto Kuhler's baggage-Tip Top Tap kept the baggage room up front and the tap lounge aft, wrapped in his ribbed sides. Kuhler gave the whole train one look, from the Hudson's shroud to the finned tail.
To check: car numbers.

MR1947_PullmanSleeper.head: Jefferson River, an 8-6-4 sleeper
text: The Olympian Hiawatha took over the Chicago - Seattle/Tacoma run on June 29, 1947: a Brooks Stevens styled streamliner on the Milwaukee Road's Pacific Extension, much of it under electric wire across the Rockies and Cascades. Most cars came from the Menomonee Valley shops; the sleepers and Skytop sleeper-lounges came from Pullman-Standard in 1948-49. Pullman-Standard built the 'River' series sleepers on an order of February 1946, delivered October - December 1948. Each held eight duplex roomettes (their windows alternate high and low), six roomettes and four double bedrooms. This model is 24 Jefferson River, which later ran as Kansas City Southern 107 and RPCX 24 and is preserved today.

MR1935_BeaverTail.head: The first Beaver Tail
text: On May 29, 1935 the Milwaukee Road started the Hiawatha between Chicago, St. Paul and Minneapolis: about 410 miles in six and a half hours, behind new streamlined Class A 4-4-2 Atlantics built for sustained running at 100 mph. The cars were not bought from Pullman or Budd - they were designed and welded together in the railroad's own Milwaukee Shops, in the Menomonee Valley, a lightweight-car programme the shops had begun in 1934.

The train ended in a parlor-observation car with a rounded, sloping tail that soon earned the nickname 'Beaver Tail'. The rear area seated 24, and the car had separate men's and women's lounges. Two were built, named Nokomis and Wenonah after characters in Longfellow's 'Song of Hiawatha' - the poem that gave the train its name.
The rear windows were small, so passengers in the observation end saw less of the track than the shape promised. Later Beaver Tails changed the layout, and the 1939 finned cars went further still.
To check: the shape of the tail windows against photos; the model's tail follows the fleet template.

MR1942_WarBondCoach.head: Buy War Bonds

'Buy War Bonds' ran along the lower side in gold leaf, and each side carried 48 white stars, one for each state: 24 on the letterboard and 24 on the skirting. The road name was left off to make room.

Orange and maroon were blended in at each end so the car would sit comfortably in an orange train. After its dedication at Chicago Union Station on 1 October the car toured the system and then went to work on the Afternoon Hiawatha.

MR1948_SkytopParlor.head: The Rapids Skytops
text: On May 29, 1948 - thirteen years to the day after the first Hiawatha - the Milwaukee Road put new Brooks Stevens styled Morning and Afternoon Hiawathas into service between Chicago and the Twin Cities, built almost entirely by its own Milwaukee Shops. The best-known cars the Milwaukee Shops ever built. Brooks Stevens' Skytop parlor-lounges ended the Morning and Afternoon Hiawathas from May 29, 1948: the rear of the car is about 90% glass - 27 windows of 15 different shapes rising into the ceiling - over a 12-seat solarium, with 24 parlor chairs and a four-seat drawing room ahead of it. Inside they were paneled in wood.

Four were built: 186 Cedar Rapids, 187 Coon Rapids, 188 Dell Rapids and 189 Priest Rapids. They were retired in 1970. Cedar Rapids survives and still runs with the Friends of the 261. The model follows MPL floor plan A-4470 revision E.

MR1947_SkytopSleeper.head: The Creek Skytops
text: The Olympian Hiawatha took over the Chicago - Seattle/Tacoma run on June 29, 1947: a Brooks Stevens styled streamliner on the Milwaukee Road's Pacific Extension, much of it under electric wire across the Rockies and Cascades. Most cars came from the Menomonee Valley shops; the sleepers and Skytop sleeper-lounges came from Pullman-Standard in 1948-49. The train was never a money-maker against the Great Northern and Northern Pacific, and it was withdrawn in May 1961.

The Olympian's tail car was a Pullman-Standard Skytop sleeper-lounge, built December 1948 - January 1949. Eight double bedrooms lined one side of the car, with an observation lounge for 19 in the glass tail. Unlike the shop-built Skytop parlors they had no wood paneling, and they carried a fluted stainless tail band with 'Olympian Hiawatha' script.

Six were built, in the 'Creek' series: 12 Alder Creek, 14 Arrow Creek, 15 Coffee Creek, 16 Gold Creek, 17 Marble Creek and 18 Spanish Creek. All went to Canadian National in 1964. The plan comes from MPL drawing A-4226; the lounge glass and stainless band from book photos.

MR1939_FinnedBeaverTail.head: The finned Beaver Tail
text: For 1938-39 the Milwaukee Road hired industrial designer Otto Kuhler to restyle the Hiawatha. The shops built a new train with heavily ribbed sides, and the Atlantics gave way to Kuhler-shrouded Class F7 4-6-4 Hudsons. In January 1939 the railroad split the service into a Morning and an Afternoon Hiawatha, so two full trainsets were needed.

The best known of all the Beaver Tails. Kuhler added fins at the rear and continued the ribbing along the sides; inside, an exterior-facing sofa in the solarium let passengers watch the track run away behind them. The lounge seated 28 and the solarium 17. Four were built: Earling, Merrill, Miller and Mitchell.
The finned cars ran on the Hiawathas until the 1948 Skytops replaced them, and then went on to other trains.
To check: the fin shape - the model's fins are a PLACEHOLDER until a drawing or a good side photo is found.
